title: How Alaska Airlines leans into local at Alaska Lounges
summary: Travel writer Chris Dong takes readers inside Alaska Lounges, where signature comforts pair with design, food and drinks inspired by each destination.
body_markdown:
Portland’s main terminal, which opened in 2024, was one of the first U.S. airports designed to fully embrace biophilic design, an approach that builds indoor spaces around the natural world. Living trees and plants fill the hall, and dozens of skylights let daylight stream in.


The Alaska Lounge sits on a mezzanine right in the middle of it all. The roughly 14,000-square-foot space opened in June 2026, with glass partitions along its edge that look straight down into the terminal.


When I first entered at ground level, I passed a mural of Mount Hood, which artist Ben Butler crafted from layered wood. Upstairs, the timber roof felt close enough to touch, a bit like stepping into a treehouse.


Walnut slats create distinct spaces within the lounge, and signature Alaska Airlines blue and green provide a splash of color. From one of Alaska’s club chairs, I could see the airfield and forested Portland hills, framed by floor-to-ceiling windows.


Beyond the design, the amenities lean local, too. The coffee bar pours Stumptown, the Portland roaster, which makes a blend just for Alaska. Portland breweries are often on tap, including Backwoods and Hopworks. The kitchen also turns out a build-your-own crepe station at breakfast and a seasonal menu featuring a spring pea tortellini in lemon-herb cream later in the day.
